source.title: Scaling Parameter-Constrained Language Models with Quality Data
source.authors: Er-Nie Chang; Matteo Paltenghi; Yang Li; Pin-Jie Lin; Changsheng Zhao; Patrick Huber; Ze-Chun Liu; Rastislav Rabatin; Yang-Yang Shi; Vikas Chandra

record.tranche_reason: The paper trains models across parameter and token counts and records evaluation loss, and it fits a data-quality-adjusted relation for reasoning accuracy. This is a different measurement and formulation from the original loss-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports evaluation-loss values for runs in Table G, so selected loss results are recorded below. Its primary fitted scaling relation predicts average accuracy using effective tokens; it does not fit or test power-law loss exponents, predict the loss of much larger runs, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Other reported values for training loss and task accuracy are not all reproduced as individual rows because of the row limit.
record.test_reason: The study trains 210 runs of 25M–1.5B models and fits a Chinchilla-form law with quality-adjusted tokens to average zero-shot accuracy on eight reasoning tasks. It reports how well the fit tracks true accuracy, which bears on V6. Its eval-loss table comes from heavily repeated data (about 9.5–48 epochs), so it does not cleanly test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that effective training tokens, adjusted for diversity and syntheticity, capture data quality in a Chinchilla-form law for reasoning accuracy, with in-sample Pearson +0.83. Quality gains matter most for 25M–500M models, while raw token count dominates for larger, data-hungry models. They note that the limited number of sample points restricts the reliability of the constants.
record.recipe_differences: The paper replaces loss as the fitted target with average reasoning-task accuracy and introduces an effective-token adjustment based on data diversity and syntheticity; it does not reproduce the original loss-scaling or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported evaluation loss and accuracy vary with data refinement, data percentage/token count, and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective tokens weighted by diversity (compression ratio) and syntheticity (teacher perplexity) better account for accuracy. Quality matters more for 25M–500M models; token count dominates at larger sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data quality acts as a multiplier on effective training tokens in scaling relations.

fits_no_version.finding: Under heavy repetition on small subsets, eval loss rises with model size even as train loss approaches zero (e.g., Selection+Synthesis 10%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a strongly data-repeated regime, larger models overfit and held-out loss is non-monotonic in parameters.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Evaluation-loss values are tabulated without a fitted loss law or uncertainty estimates. The paper states that the number of sample points limits the precision and reliability of its estimated constants. The reported accuracy correlation is not described as independent held-out validation.
record.rows_left_out: Table G reports many further model-size, data-percentage and refinement combinations. Due to the 60-row cap, the record retains selected full size sweeps for five data conditions and omits the remaining evaluation-loss rows, as well as the separate training-loss and per-run accuracy values in Appendix G.

untested.parts: No power-law fit to loss. Loss is reported only under heavy data repetition, so the condition that the other factors are not bottlenecks is not met.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
Text pretraining only. The repeated-data regime is present, but no power-law fit is tested on it.
No held-out or extrapolated prediction. Only eight commonsense tasks, averaged; no per-task predictability.
Alternative Dq forms change the fit quality (R² 0.19–0.45), but this concerns an accuracy law, not loss exponents or the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Per-run average accuracy by model size and token count, e.g. Random 100%: 38.27 at 25M to 48.23 at 1.5B, with a dip at 50M
missing.locator: Appendix G table, Avg. Acc. column; Figs. 6–7

missing.what: Fitted constants (A=-0.8546, B=-18.31, E=1.14, α=0.045, β=0.368, c1, c2) compared with Besiroglu et al.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope label was dropped: all loss rows are cannot_determine. The loss comes from runs with many epochs on small subsets, where data is the bottleneck V1 excludes. The paper also states constants with bootstrapped standard errors only for Besiroglu, not for its own fit.

versions.untested_parts: The paper records evaluation loss across its runs but does not fit a power law to loss or establish behavior over several orders of magnitude with the other factors non-bottlenecking.
No test of whether small-run fits predict much larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Experiments are text pretraining; no other modality or training regime is tested.

Prediction is evaluated for average zero-shot accuracy on eight reasoning tasks and the paper's sampled data and models; broader downstream task families and independent held-out scaling-law validation are not established.
The paper adds data-quality terms, but does not compare fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor report a systematic bend away from a single loss power law.

rows.subject: 210 data points across model sizes and data samples
rows.operation_detail: Fit the proposed accuracy relation and compare predicted with true average accuracy.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between predicted and true average accuracy
rows.locator: Section 7, Figure 5; Appendix D
rows.note: The paper reports this correlation across model sizes and data samples; it does not describe this as an independent held-out prediction test.
rows.check: Pearson +0.83 is in-sample: the same 210 points were used to fit the constants. Appendix Table 2 gives R²=0.45 for the chosen Dq form, which is weaker than r=0.83 implies. Read the state as observed in-sample only.

relationships.condition: Average zero-shot accuracy on eight reasoning tasks, 25M–1.5B models, RefinedWeb-derived data, in-sample fit
relationships.reason: The fitted N and Dq law tracks true average accuracy with Pearson +0.83. Accuracy generally rises with model size and tokens, per Table G and Fig. 5 (r35).
relationships.display_finding: The fitted model-size and data-quality law correlates with observed average accuracy at Pearson r = 0.83, with accuracy generally increasing with size and tokens.

relationships.condition: Same fit; dependence on data quality and functional form
relationships.reason: Text-based: predictability needs a fitted data-quality adjustment. The chosen form explains only R²=0.45 (Table 2), other forms 0.19–0.35, and validation is in-sample only (r35).
relationships.display_finding: The fitted data-quality adjustment achieved R²=0.45 versus 0.19–0.35 for alternative forms, with validation confined to the fitting data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: The fitted accuracy relation has a reported Pearson correlation of +0.83 between predicted and true accuracy on these data (r35).
